hook

A twenty-five-year-old walked into a New York bank and asked for twenty-two million dollars. She said she was a German heiress with a sixty million euro fortune. She lived in five-star hotels, tipped with hundred dollar bills, and flew on private jets. There was just one problem. The fortune did not exist. And in the end, it wasn't the police who caught her. It was a friend who was still waiting to be paid back. This is the story of Anna Delvey.
arrive

New York, 2013. A young woman lands in the city during fashion week. She was meant to stay for a few days. She never went home. She had no job and no apartment. What she did have was a suitcase of designer clothes, and a story. Her name, she said, was Anna Delvey. Her family back in Germany was rich, and one day the money would all be hers.
life

And New York believed her. She ate at the best restaurants. She handed waiters and doormen hundred dollar bills, and hotel staff competed to help her. She got invited to the right parties, full of artists, bankers and millionaires. Nobody asked where the money came from. In that world, asking felt rude. And that silence was exactly what she needed.
club

Because Anna had a dream. A private club for the art world, called the Anna Delvey Foundation. Galleries, a restaurant, and a members-only lounge, all under one roof. She even picked the building, a six-story landmark on Park Avenue South called the Church Missions House. All she needed was money. A lot of it.
bank

So she asked a Manhattan bank for a loan of twenty-two million dollars. As proof, she showed statements from Swiss accounts holding sixty million euros. She had made them herself. When the bank had questions, the answers came by email from her financial adviser in Germany, a man named Peter Hennecke. He confirmed everything. But Peter Hennecke wasn't real. The emails came from Anna. The bank turned the loan down, but it still gave her a hundred thousand dollar overdraft. She used it to pay lawyers at an investment firm to work on her deal. When they asked to verify her fortune, she backed out, and about fifty-five thousand dollars came back to her.
tricks

Then the bills started piling up. She lived in a boutique hotel in SoHo and charged everything to her room. By the time the staff asked about it, the tab was around thirty thousand dollars. She deposited a hundred and sixty thousand dollars in checks that would bounce, and took out about seventy thousand before the bank caught on. She chartered a private jet to an investors' conference in Omaha, and the thirty-five thousand dollar bill was never paid. Every time, the trick was the same. Act rich, move fast, and be gone before anyone checks.
morocco

In May 2017, Anna invited three people on a dream trip to Marrakech. Her personal trainer, a videographer, and her friend Rachel, a photo editor at Vanity Fair. Remember Rachel. They stayed in a private villa at one of the most famous hotels in Morocco, at around seven thousand dollars a night. Anna said everything was on her. Then, at the end of the week, her cards stopped working. The managers grew impatient, and Anna turned to Rachel. Could she put it on her card, just for now? Rachel agreed. The charges came to about sixty-two thousand dollars, more than Rachel earned in a year.
trap

Back in New York, Rachel waited. Anna always had a reason. A delayed transfer. A problem with her trust fund. Weeks went by, and only five thousand dollars came back. Meanwhile, Anna's world was cracking. Hotels threw her out. The jet company went to the police. And then Anna disappeared. She told Rachel she was at a luxury rehab clinic in Malibu. So Rachel went to the authorities, and helped set a trap. On October third, 2017, Anna stepped out of the clinic, expecting lunch with her friend. Instead, the police were waiting.
truth

Then the real story came out. There was no German fortune. Her real name was Anna Sorokin. She was born near Moscow in 1991, and her father had been a truck driver. When she was a teenager, her family moved to Germany. She left an art school in London, interned at a fashion magazine in Paris, and somewhere along the way, Anna Sorokin became Anna Delvey. She wasn't born rich. She simply decided to act like it.
trial

In 2019 she went on trial in Manhattan, and even there, she dressed the part. A stylist picked her courtroom outfits. Her lawyer argued she was just faking it until she made it, like so many people in New York. The jury found her guilty on eight charges, including grand larceny. But in a twist, she was cleared of stealing from Rachel, because Rachel had handed over her own card. The sentence was four to twelve years in prison. Asked if she had any regrets, she said she would be lying if she said she was sorry for anything.
end

And here is the strangest part. While she sat in jail, Netflix paid her three hundred and twenty thousand dollars for her story. Much of it went to paying back the people she owed. She left prison in 2021, and was soon detained by immigration officers for overstaying her visa. In 2022, the series Inventing Anna was watched around the world. Later, she even competed on a TV dance show while wearing her ankle monitor, and was voted off in the very first week. She pretended to be rich and famous. In the end, the pretending made her famous.
